video_title: No Code Is Code: Zapier CEO Wade Foster on Headless Tools, Zapier MCP & Automation Bench
gist: Zapier co-founder and CEO Wade Foster argues knowledge work is consolidating around a single per-person 'daily driver' AI harness such as Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT, so automation platforms must go headless and ship into those harnesses via MCP rather than trying to be the destination. He reports that the best frontier model tops out near 40% on Zapier's roughly 600-task Automation Bench, that about 80% of what customers currently delegate to agents should be deterministic code, and that the binding constraint on the market is not rival tooling but that most businesses still have no idea what to use AI for.

insights.claim: Wade Foster says the dominant AI usage pattern that emerged over the past 18 months is each knowledge worker settling on a single 'daily driver' harness — Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT — where most of their work happens, rather than AI diffusing evenly into every existing SaaS product.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Software vendors whose roadmap assumes users will come to their own UI are mispricing distribution risk; the defensible position is being callable from whatever harness the user already lives in.
insights.quote: most folks seem to have adopted their own daily AI driver tool. Maybe this is claude code, maybe this is cursor, maybe this is chatbt, you name it.

insights.claim: Foster states the market has split between platforms trying to force users to build agents on their own platform and platforms going headless so context can be brought anywhere, and that the headless strategy is the winning one — citing Salesforce as an example of the headless posture.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A useful screen for enterprise software holdings: which vendors are exposing their data and actions outward versus trying to trap workflows on-platform.
insights.quote: then you see like the sales forces of the world that are like we're headless you can bring it wherever you want etc and I definitely think that ladder is the winning strategy

insights.claim: Foster personally uses Cursor as his daily driver and pipes Zapier's internal employee harness into it via MCP, where that harness supplies a virtual file system acting as a context layer plus automations and deployable apps.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A CEO of a non-engineering-first company running his day inside a coding IDE signals that coding harnesses are becoming general-purpose work environments, expanding the addressable market for Cursor-like products well beyond developers.

insights.claim: Foster predicts the last decade's SaaS explosion is being followed by an explosion of headless tools, with the new twist that the harness itself can build some of those tools on demand.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Expect SaaS packaging to be repriced around API and MCP surface rather than UI seats; products with no headless surface face structural decline.
insights.quote: now it feels like there's this almost explosion of headless tools that is happening

insights.claim: Foster argues that just because a harness can build a tool does not mean it should, because self-built tools transfer maintenance, reliability and uptime burden onto the user — leaving real room for third-party application-layer companies.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: The 'AI will just build all your software' bear case for app-layer SaaS understates ongoing operational cost; durable vendors sell reliability, not just capability.
insights.quote: yes, it can build it, but should you have it build it? Because now you're accepting a certain amount of maintenance, a certain amount of reliability, a certain amount of uptime

insights.claim: Foster claims model labs are structurally handicapped in the harness and aggregation layer because they cannot sell each other's tokens or open-source tokens, creating room for a neutral third party to wrangle multi-model capability.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis that model-agnostic orchestration layers capture durable value even as labs push up-stack into applications.
insights.quote: they're going to struggle because they can't sell tokens from each other or from open source or all that sort of thing

themes.theme: Automation Bench scores and model ceilings

insights.claim: Zapier runs Automation Bench, a benchmark of roughly 600 real knowledge-work tasks spanning marketing, sales, HR and operations, used to score frontier models on business automation rather than coding or reasoning.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A vendor-run benchmark on genuine enterprise workflows is a better read on white-collar automation timelines than the coding and reasoning evals that dominate headlines.

insights.claim: Astra, described as GPT6 and released the week before the interview, set a new state of the art on Zapier's Automation Bench at only about 40% of tasks completed accurately — meaning the best available model fails the majority of ordinary business tasks.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A hard ceiling datapoint against near-term white-collar displacement narratives; the gap between model capability headlines and deployable business automation remains wide, and Foster notes the benchmark is nowhere near saturated.
insights.quote: last week Astra came out GPT6. It's the new state-of-the-art on that model. It performs about 40% of the tasks accurately which is the highest that there is.

insights.claim: Gemini 37 scores below Astra on Automation Bench but at a fraction of the cost, creating a live cost-performance frontier along which buyers must trade task by task, and Foster says modern organizations will demand the ability to swap models per workflow.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Cheap good-enough models will win the bulk of automation volume while frontier models get reserved for hard tasks, which matters for how inference revenue mix is modeled.
insights.quote: it's more expensive than say something like Gemini 37, which is does pretty good, but does it at a fraction of the cost

insights.claim: Zapier is building Automation Bench v2 specifically to measure how much tool access lifts model scores and how much it cuts cost and latency, rather than only scoring bare models.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: If tool-augmented scores materially exceed bare-model scores, it is quantified evidence that value accrues to the tooling layer and not only to the model layer.

insights.claim: Zapier's stated product goal is that installing Zapier alongside an agent produces measurably better benchmark output than the model alone, turning benchmark lift into the company's core sales proof point.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A falsifiable, quantified value claim is an unusual and potentially defensible go-to-market posture in agent tooling; watch whether the v2 numbers substantiate it.
insights.quote: we are making sure that when you install Zapier alongside of your agent that you're actually getting better output on these benchmarks than you would if you were just using the models alone

insights.claim: A representative Automation Bench task requires marking a closed deal as won, routing a win notice per routing policy, confirming account tier from a spreadsheet hierarchy, converting currencies and checking open support escalations — multi-hop work requiring policy retrieval, not single-step actions.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Shows the failure mode is context assembly and policy compliance rather than raw reasoning, which favors vendors with deep connector and permissions coverage over pure model quality.

insights.claim: Foster estimates roughly 80% of what Zapier customers currently use agents for should instead be plain deterministic code, because code is cheaper and more reliable for those steps.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Implies inference demand from enterprise agent deployments is inflated by misuse and could compress as buyers optimize — a risk to naive token-growth extrapolations.
insights.quote: the vast majority of what people are using an agent for 80% in fact they probably should be using actually old-fashioned deterministic code

insights.claim: Foster's design principle is that the agent should build and maintain the workflow while what actually runs in production stays a deterministic workflow with AI interwoven only where reasoning is genuinely required.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A concrete architecture pattern for enterprise AI ROI: pay for intelligence at build time rather than at every runtime execution.
insights.quote: the agent almost take over the human role of building and maintaining it, but what is actually running is still a very deterministic workflow with AI interwoven in like the places that is most necessary

insights.claim: Foster declares no-code as a category antiquated and says the successor is code generated and maintained by agents, summarized as 'the new no code is code'.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Directly bearish for no-code vendors whose moat is a visual builder UI, and notable because the CEO of the canonical no-code automation company is calling the paradigm dead.
insights.quote: the idea of building a no code it feels antiquated to me. It's like the new co no code is code.

insights.claim: Foster argues visual workflow representation survives not as an authoring interface but as a verification and documentation surface, letting humans confirm the agent built what they intended and share it with colleagues.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Reframes UI value from creation to auditability: the enduring product surface in agent-built software is inspection, not drag-and-drop.

insights.claim: Foster expects a persistent long-run split in which some jobs are permanently better served by deterministic code on reliability and cost, with only the remainder needing 'the ghost in the machine'.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Argues against a total-token-consumption endgame; a durable share of enterprise automation stays non-inference workload.
insights.quote: I struggle to think of a world where there are just certain jobs that like deterministic code is still going to be more reliable and cheap

insights.claim: Foster notes that when a hardened deterministic workflow fails, an agent can be sent to troubleshoot and repair either that instance or the workflow itself, a self-healing pattern that changes the economics of maintaining automation at scale.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Self-healing pipelines relax the human ops headcount that historically capped how many automations a company could run, expanding automation volume per employee.

insights.claim: Foster's view is that most AI companies' real competitor is not each other but customer ignorance, since the average user has barely tried anything beyond ChatGPT, Gemini inside Google search, or Microsoft Copilot at work.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Implies default-distribution incumbents currently own the mainstream AI relationship, and that market expansion beats share-shifting as a growth strategy for challengers.
insights.quote: most of us our competition isn't each other. It isn't the the tools that you talked about. It's do people actually know what to do with these tools yet?

insights.claim: Foster warns that observers who live on X overweight micro-differences between models and products that mainstream buyers are entirely unaware of, distorting competitive analysis.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A sanity check on sentiment-driven AI positioning: benchmark leadership rarely converts into mainstream share on the timeline that online consensus assumes.
insights.quote: if all if you hang out on X all day because on X we're all just hyper aware of what model came out, what tools gaining traction, who just raised a huge bunch of money

insights.claim: Foster says the automation market turned out to be roughly a thousand times bigger than he assumed when founding Zapier 15 years ago, and that plenty of room remains among customers who know none of the competing AI tools.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Supports long-duration TAM expansion for workflow automation rather than a zero-sum share war among known vendors.
insights.quote: The market for automation was like orders of magnitude bigger than I ever thought it was when we started the company 15 years ago. It's probably a thousand times bigger than what we set out.

insights.claim: Foster invokes Paul Graham's YC-era advice that startups rarely compete with Google's or Facebook's founders but with a mid-level product director on a two-year promo clock, and applies it to OpenAI and Anthropic now that they are big tech that cannot build everything.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A reusable frame for handicapping lab-versus-startup competition: labs will be world-best at models and merely adequate at most adjacent products.
insights.quote: you're not often competing directly with Google you're not going toe-to-toe with Larry and Sergey you're not going toe-to-toe with Zuck

insights.claim: Foster describes a 'sea of sameness' among AI tooling startups as a real present-day challenge, meaning differentiation pressure is intense even while end-user adoption remains low.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Crowded undifferentiated supply alongside latent demand implies a shakeout decided by distribution and customer education, not feature sets.
insights.quote: There's a there's a sort of sea of sameness out there that is a real challenge at the moment.

insights.claim: Host Nathan Labenz says he has been clearly wrong in expecting far more economy-wide change in how work gets done, noting that despite Astra-level capability and exploded model-company revenue, ordinary people's days are unchanged and they use chatbots mostly for meal planning, vacations and workouts.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: A capability-versus-diffusion gap this wide means lab revenue growth is running far ahead of measurable productivity effects, which matters for how long AI capex can be justified by end usage.
insights.quote: revenue has exploded at the model companies obviously but like we don't see nearly as much change as I would have guessed

insights.claim: Foster identifies recommendations — telling users what they should actually automate — as one of Zapier's hardest unsolved problems across its entire history, and the place he now thinks AI can finally break through.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: If AI solves use-case discovery, activation rates for automation platforms could step-change; this is the metric to watch in Zapier-like businesses.
insights.quote: one of the hardest problems of Zapier, even till this day, has been helping people with recommendations. What actually should you use this stuff for?

insights.claim: Foster explains adoption inertia as habit-based rather than capability-based: people repeat yesterday's workflow from muscle memory, so AI must be dramatically better rather than marginally better to dislodge them.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Predicts step-function rather than gradual adoption curves, and favors products that surface personalized dramatically-better options over incremental improvements.
insights.quote: We are creatures of habit and so we wake up and we go about our day the same way we did but the day before

insights.claim: Foster runs a weekly personal automation that reviews his activity across Gmail, Slack, the browser and his chat harness and proposes specific tools he should build, and says it has produced new systems automating parts of his job nearly every week since the start of the year.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable pattern for compounding personal automation, and Foster says it is very likely Zapier will productize it in some form for customers.
insights.quote: I started doing this workflow at the beginning of the year and pretty much every week now I have new tools, new systems that start to automate bits and pieces of my job

insights.claim: Zapier's activity-watching approach reads API event streams from connected apps rather than screen-recording the user, a choice Foster attributes to Zapier's existing API competence emerging naturally rather than to a principled design argument.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Leaves an opening for screen-recording rivals offering a single install, versus Zapier's requirement that users connect many accounts before getting any insight.
insights.quote: we're good at APIs and we're good at that stuff. And so that was like just an easy natural just was an emergent experience experiment an emergent property.

insights.claim: Foster argues automation recommendations only need to be about 50% good to be valuable, because their real function is provoking the user to react and start brainstorming.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Lowers the accuracy bar for shipping recommendation features, implying current-generation models are already sufficient for this product category.
insights.quote: half half the battle is just getting you to react to something. Even if the ideas aren't perfect, they only need to be like 50% good enough

themes.theme: Proprietary data moats and multi-agent loops

insights.claim: Zapier's internal auto-email program spins up five independent agents to evaluate each troubleshooting situation, and Zapier found that when four of the five agree the diagnosis is usually correct.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Ensemble agreement as a confidence signal is a practical reliability technique that raises usable accuracy without waiting for better models, at the cost of roughly 5x inference spend.
insights.quote: it spins up five agents independent agents that evaluate the troubleshooting situation. And we notice that when four of the five agents tend to agree, there's a pretty good chance that's actually the the issue

insights.claim: Zapier's improvement loop is deliberately unfancy: human auditors give each agent output a thumbs up or thumbs down with a written reason, and those reasons feed back into the system on repeat.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Suggests the operational moat in agent products is disciplined labeled-preference data collection rather than novel retrieval or model architecture.
insights.quote: A lot of this is not particularly fancy at the end of the day. It's just take the example, did you like it? Did you not like it? And just rinse, wash, and repeat.

insights.claim: Foster argues incumbents hold a real advantage in the AI era if they can wield proprietary data to build products the models alone cannot match, pushing back on the assumption that AI uniformly favors startups.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Supports allocating toward data-rich incumbents that are actually shipping AI, rather than assuming disruption of every installed base.
insights.quote: this is where a lot of the incumbents have an advantage is if they're able to yield that to actually build a better product at the end of the day that the models alone can't do

insights.claim: Foster notes that simply connecting a model to a user's Gmail history makes it write markedly better email with no workflow tuning at all, illustrating how cheaply company or personal data converts into model performance.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Data connection is the highest-ROI first step in enterprise AI, ahead of fine-tuning or prompt engineering budgets.
insights.quote: it's just by hooking up your company's data, all of a sudden the models get better

themes.theme: Pricing shift from seats to usage and outcomes

insights.claim: Foster states that seat-based pricing is dead or dying, because when intelligence is a core part of the product experience a fixed per-seat fee makes no economic sense.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the revenue model of most public SaaS names; expect seat-count guidance to become a less meaningful growth metric.
insights.quote: by and large when you're when intelligence is such a core part of these product experiences, I don't see how a fixed seatbased pricing mechanism really makes much sense for that at all

insights.claim: Foster's pricing framework splits by positioning: commodity-oriented products land on usage-based pricing, the 'intelligence on tap' utility framing he associates with Sam Altman, while enterprise-oriented products push toward outcome pricing such as per-resolved-ticket billing in customer support.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A screen for which AI vendors can actually charge per outcome — only those whose success is cleanly demarcated; everyone else reverts to metered usage and thinner margins.

insights.claim: Foster cautions that most current AI products stop one or two steps short of truly delivering an outcome, which pulls them back into pure usage-based pricing despite outcome pricing being more attractive.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Tempers enthusiasm for outcome-pricing narratives in AI software; much of what is marketed as outcome pricing is likely repackaged usage pricing.
insights.quote: It's you kind of stop one one or two steps shy of truly delivering the outcome. you were like part of delivering a piece of the outcome.

insights.claim: Foster frames the whole shift as software converging on selling work, with buyers eventually managing an explicit budget for work to be done rather than a software license budget.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: If software budgets migrate into labor budgets, the addressable spend pool for AI vendors is services-sized rather than software-sized.
insights.quote: it's basically selling work of some portion at the end of the day

insights.claim: Asked whether model companies' subscription plans amount to price discrimination, with Claude Max and OpenAI Pro users effectively getting far more tokens per dollar than API buyers, Foster declines to endorse any rule and cites free markets while explicitly invoking Microsoft's bundling dominance as the cautionary precedent.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Token price discrimination between consumer plans and API access is a live margin threat to third-party AI value-add services, and the ecosystem appears unlikely to organize against it.
insights.quote: I think many of us lived through and are still living through like Microsoft's dominance and how they use bundling to their advantage to box out better products candidly

themes.theme: Org design, AI fluency and token governance

insights.claim: Zapier reached roughly 100% daily AI usage across its employee base within about a year of ChatGPT's launch, so technical adoption is no longer its constraint.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Sets a benchmark for what full internal AI fluency looks like and redirects attention to the harder second-stage problem of production-grade workflows.
insights.quote: we got within a year or so basically of chatt launching almost like 100% of the employee base is using AI dayto-day

insights.claim: Foster says Zapier's current AI bottleneck is organizational rather than technical — rewriting job descriptions, rethinking compensation, moving and dissolving teams, and retraining people — which is why he assigned AI transformation to chief people officer Brandon.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: The second phase of enterprise AI value is an HR and org-design problem, so demand for change management and reskilling may run ahead of demand for more tooling.
insights.quote: the challenges start to look like a lot more like people issues where it's like okay we kind of have to rewrite certain job descriptions. We have to rethink how we do compensation.

insights.claim: Foster explicitly does not recommend the chief-people-officer-owns-AI model to other companies, saying it could just as easily have been the CMO and that leaders should assign AI transformation to whoever fits their specific bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Counters the emerging best-practice narrative around a designated AI transformation owner; the right answer is bottleneck-dependent, not role-dependent.

insights.claim: Zapier moved toward public-by-default internal communications partly because its AI agents are substantially more effective when they can see Slack context, and it shifted the norm via a friendly executive-team competition rather than a mandate.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Agent effectiveness now creates direct economic pressure toward internal transparency, a new and non-obvious driver of corporate information policy.
insights.quote: our AI agents were just so much more effective when they were able to see the context inside of Slack

insights.claim: Foster claims most people vastly overestimate how much internal communication genuinely needs to be private and underestimate the gains when humans and agents can see a company's full working context; Zapier keeps only matters like HR incidents and active security vulnerabilities private.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Actionable org policy: the default-private posture of most companies is now a measurable tax on AI effectiveness.
insights.quote: most people far overestimate the number of things where that is required and definitely underestimate the power of what happens when both humans and agents have access to the full context of what a company is working on

insights.claim: Some Zapier engineers are spending $30,000 a month on tokens, which Foster calls outliers, and Zapier still sets no individual token budgets — only self-service dashboards showing employees their spend and the cost difference between powerful and cheaper models.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A concrete upper bound on per-engineer inference spend at a mid-size company, useful for modeling enterprise inference revenue per seat.

insights.claim: Foster predicts token budgets will become a real management construct with differentiated allocations, where more AI-fluent employees get larger budgets because they extract more output per dollar.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Token allocation as a performance-linked resource implies a new category of FinOps tooling for AI spend attribution inside companies.
insights.quote: like this person is going to get a higher budget than this person because they know how to get higher like output from those things

insights.claim: Foster reports that in a nearly 800-person organization the main lever on runaway token spend is education, since high spenders split between the genuinely productive and those reaching for Fable or Astro where a cheaper approach would do.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Model-selection training is a direct cost lever; enterprises that route tasks well should show materially lower AI cost per seat than peers.
insights.quote: when you have a almost 800 person organization, you're there's just a big education effort involved

insights.claim: Zapier has flattened management layers and needs fewer dedicated data analysts because everyone is their own analyst, yet Foster stresses strong management remains crucial and remaining analysts moved to higher-value work.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: The observable AI org effect so far is role compression and wider spans of control, not headcount elimination — a more modest displacement signal than consensus assumes.
insights.quote: there's definitely been like a flattening of management layers. Uh, but strong management is still crucial. We're not getting rid of managers anytime soon, but managers can handle a higher volume.

insights.claim: Foster says the classic engineering-product-design team structure is largely gone at Zapier even though the individual roles still exist, with work becoming far more malleable across those boundaries.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Role boundaries dissolving before roles disappear is a leading indicator of AI's org impact, visible well before headcount changes show up in filings.
insights.quote: the idea of like a classic traditional EPD like that's largely gone

insights.claim: Foster's forward-looking org model is employees building the factory that builds the product — a software factory, a support factory — where AI runs the inner loop and humans design the system, with human-in-the-loop steps progressively removed as models improve.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A concrete template for what an AI-native company looks like, and a test for whether a company's AI initiatives are structural or cosmetic.
insights.quote: the team shifting more into building the factory that builds the products and the company and the marketing

themes.theme: Credential security and AI co-authorship norms

insights.claim: Foster notes Zapier has custodied user credentials to third-party services for 15 years, but what is new is security-capable models that patiently loop over issue after issue until they find vulnerabilities in any software project.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Every software project's latent vulnerabilities become discoverable at once, implying a discrete step-up in disclosed breaches and in security spend across SaaS.
insights.quote: you do have like these mythos caliber like security models that are able to patiently just loop over issue after issue and find things

insights.claim: Foster's base case is a one-time reacclimation investment in security followed by a return to a steady-state offense-versus-defense posture, since the same models that find vulnerabilities also make them easier to patch.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A relatively benign framing versus catastrophist cyber narratives; implies a spending spike rather than a permanent regime change in security budgets.
insights.quote: it feels like there's this almost one-time like investment to reaclimate and then you kind of get back to more steady state of like offense versus defense

insights.claim: Host Nathan Labenz argues that early access to frontier lab capabilities could become a real competitive differentiator for credential-holding companies, since a vendor inside all the early-access clubs can find and fix issues faster than a startup that is not, and Foster confirms Zapier wants the earliest access it can get.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Lab access privileges may become a durable, hard-to-replicate advantage for incumbents in any credential-custody business.

insights.claim: Foster's stance on AI-written communication is that using AI is fine and low quality is the actual problem, because low-judgment people can now generate high volumes of low-quality material that overwhelms readers.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-slop debate for managers: police quality and ownership rather than tool usage or AI-detection scores.
insights.quote: it's not using AI is not the problem. It's like low quality that's the fight at the end of the day

insights.claim: Zapier's internal guidelines for AI-assisted communication require owning what you send, spending more time authoring than the reader spends reading, understanding your own content well enough to answer questions on it, making asks explicit, and verifying details.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: A directly copyable corporate AI-usage policy that targets accountability rather than prohibition.
insights.quote: you need to own what you send. If you wrote it, you probably should be putting more time into authoring the thing than the reader is reading it.

insights.claim: Foster warns that AI summaries of summaries compound errors and that agents with broad access can pull adjacent-but-wrong context, such as a related project from three months ago, which then propagates as incorrect information through an organization.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: Retrieval-adjacency error is a distinct and underrated failure mode from hallucination, making verification layers a real product need as agent context access widens.
insights.quote: these AI summaries take an AI summary of a summary and of a summary and all of a sudden before you know it, it's actually passing on incorrect information

insights.claim: Foster says AI stylistic tells — 'it's not this, it's that', em dashes, 'the honest truth', load-bearing phrasing — make marketing material hard to stand out and require an editorial hand, even though he has no objection to AI structuring the writing.
insights.speaker: Wade Foster
insights.so_what: As AI prose saturates channels, distinctive editorial voice becomes a scarce marketing asset rather than a nice-to-have.
insights.quote: The it's not this, it's that, the M dashes, the honest truth, the loadbearing points, all that kind of stuff. I do think that is something that if you're doing that a lot, especially if you're doing in marketing material, that makes it hard to stand out.
